title: Multicore Motivation & SMP
summary: Why the industry pivoted from ever-faster single cores to putting more cores on a chip, and the symmetric multiprocessing model that resulted.

slides.markdown:
For decades, CPU clock speeds climbed steadily — but around the mid-2000s they essentially stopped, plateauing near 3–4 GHz ever since. The reason is the **power wall**: dynamic power scales roughly with clock frequency times voltage squared, and pushing frequency higher demands ever more voltage, which makes power (and heat) grow far faster than the resulting speed gain.

Past a certain point, chips simply can't dissipate the heat a faster clock would generate without exotic (and impractical) cooling — the free ride of "just raise the clock" was over.

With single-core clock speed stalled, chipmakers redirected their growing transistor budgets (still climbing per Moore's Law) toward **more cores** instead of one faster core. Two moderate-clock cores can do more total work than one core clocked unsustainably high, at a fraction of the power cost — power scales worse than linearly with frequency, but roughly linearly with core count.

This is why every mainstream CPU today — phone, laptop, server — is multicore: it was the only path left to keep delivering more compute per generation once frequency scaling hit its wall.

**Symmetric multiprocessing (SMP)** is the dominant multicore model: every core is identical, shares the same memory, and can run any task — the OS scheduler treats cores as interchangeable, not specialized. This differs from **asymmetric** designs where some cores are dedicated to specific roles.

SMP's simplicity is its strength: any thread can migrate to any core without special handling, which is exactly why it became the default for general-purpose CPUs, even as specialized big.LITTLE-style designs (fast cores + efficient cores, still symmetric in ISA) have layered on top more recently.

![An SMP layout showing multiple cores each with private L1/L2 caches, sharing an L3 cache and main memory](assets/smp-layout.svg)

Each core keeps its own private L1 and usually L2 cache for fast access to its own working set, while a larger **L3 cache** and main memory are shared across all cores — the shared layer is where cache coherence ([cache-coherence-protocols](cache-coherence-protocols)) becomes necessary.

assets.alt: An SMP layout showing multiple cores each with private L1/L2 caches, sharing an L3 cache and main memory

slides.markdown:
For years, software got faster "for free" — the same code ran quicker on next year's higher-clocked chip, no rewrite needed. Multicore ended that **free lunch**: a single-threaded program runs no faster on an 8-core chip than a 1-core one at the same clock, since nothing spread its work across the extra cores.

To benefit from more cores, software must be explicitly restructured to run in parallel — spawning threads, partitioning work — a harder engineering problem than waiting for faster hardware, which is why parallel programming became a baseline skill, not a specialty.

slides.sectionTitle: Multicore vs a hypothetical faster single core
slides.markdown:
| | One much-faster core | Multiple moderate-clock cores |
|---|---|---|
| Power/heat | Grows much faster than speed (power wall) | Scales roughly linearly with core count |
| Software needed | None — existing code just runs faster | Must be rewritten to use multiple threads |
| Best for | (Not physically achievable past a point) | Parallel/multi-tasking workloads |

**How to decide:** this isn't really a choice anymore — the power wall makes the faster-single-core path physically infeasible past current clock ceilings, so multicore is the only available lever, even though it shifts real cost onto software.

slides.sectionTitle: More cores isn't automatically more speed
slides.markdown:
It's tempting to assume doubling core count doubles performance. It doesn't, for two reasons: **Amdahl's Law** ([parallel-scalability-limits](parallel-scalability-limits)) says any serial portion caps total speedup no matter how many cores you add, and real workloads also suffer **contention** — cores fighting over shared caches, bandwidth, and locks, which worsens as core count rises.

A mostly-serial or lock-heavy program sees almost no benefit going from 4 to 32 cores — more cores only help work that was actually parallelizable.
